intro.heading: The round was observed. Did they understand the policy behind it?
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care homes.
intro.paragraph: A home runs its yearly medication administration training on a Tuesday. The senior carer who leads it watches each new carer complete a supervised round, and the manager signs the observation form. It all looks right. Then a carer asks, in passing, whether a refused dose gets recorded as missed or as refused, and the answers in the room disagree. Your written procedure says one thing. Three people remember another. Observation shows what someone does while watched. It does not show whether they have taken in the wording of your own policy.

trail.text: A senior carer runs the medication training day for four carers.
Each carer completes a supervised round and the manager observes.
Observation forms are signed and filed in the staff folders.
A carer asks how a refused dose is recorded. Two answers are given.
Four carers heard the policy once, at speed, with a round to get through.
Practice on one day with the manager watching, not understanding of the wording.
Signed forms and no record of who understood what the policy says.
“How do you know staff understand your medication policy?”

trail_close: Observed practice was never the problem. The gap is between the observation and the evidence that people understood the policy. Here is how CareStream fills it, without replacing the assessor.

why.heading: Observation shows what they do. It does not show what they know.
why.sub: Errors often start with a misread policy, so it is worth checking the reading as well as the practice.

cards.title: A policy heard once is easy to misremember
cards.body: Medication training days are busy. Carers hear your procedure while thinking about the round they are about to do, and details such as refusals or late doses slip.

cards.title: A signed form is not a check for understanding
cards.body: The form records who was watched and when. A short question set on your own wording records who understood it, and who needs another look.

cards.title: Gaps stay hidden until something goes wrong
cards.body: If nobody asks, a carer who has misread the policy keeps working to the wrong version. Errors often start there, long before anyone notices.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: Is this a medication competency assessment?
items.a: No, and we would not want you to treat it as one. Medication competence is observed in practice by a competent assessor, and that stays with you. CareStream checks whether your carers understood your own written policy. It sits alongside the observation, not in place of it.

items.q: So what does it actually check?
items.a: It checks understanding of your procedure: how your home records a refusal, who you tell about a stock problem, what you check before signing. You allocate a Medication topic module after the training day, and each carer answers short questions in the Staff Hub on their own phone.

items.q: Where do the questions come from?
items.a: From your own policies where they cover the topic, with general good practice as the fallback. You pick the topic module, not a single policy or section. You can edit and preview the lessons and questions before anyone sees them, so check them against your procedure.

items.q: What happens when a carer gets one wrong?
items.a: It goes straight into their Follow-up tab in the hub, and they get an email, at most once a day. They choose Learn & retry, a short lesson on that point followed by a fresh question, or Just retry the same question. They can retry as often as they need, and nothing is pushed at them.

items.q: Will I be told every time someone gets an answer wrong?
items.a: No. Nothing alerts you on each wrong answer. You see the picture in Analytics, under Knowledge gaps, and in a Monday digest email. That shows open gaps, staff affected, the most missed questions and how gaps are being closed.

items.q: Can staff who speak another first language use it?
items.a: Yes, on the paid plans. A carer's second language can be set by your admin, and they can open the lesson in it. The email about a wrong answer is English only, and hub menus stay in English.

items.q: Does a carer's medication certificate depend on this?
items.a: No. The free medication course on the course page has a certificate that waits for a manager observation sign off. The understanding check is separate. It is for your own policy, and it does not sign anyone off.

items.q: How much does it cost, and can I try it first?
items.a: The adhoc training screen is on the paid plans, and you can try those with a 14 day free trial. Create a free account on the registration page to look around, and see the pricing page for the current plans.

limits.heading: A check on understanding, not a competency sign off

cards.title: It does not sign anyone off as competent
cards.body: Observed practice by a competent assessor is how medication competence is judged. CareStream checks that carers understood your written policy and cannot replace the assessor or the observation.

cards.title: It does not give clinical medicines advice
cards.body: The questions test your own procedure. Decisions about doses, interactions or a particular resident belong with the prescriber, the pharmacist and your own protocols, not with a quiz.

cards.title: It does not alert you to every wrong answer
cards.body: The picture reaches you through Knowledge gaps and the Monday digest. Adhoc training and translation are on the paid plans, and the free plan does not include them.

items.q: What is the difference between a medication competency assessment and a medication quiz?
items.a: A competency assessment looks at what a person does, observed by a competent assessor. A medication quiz asks what they know. You need both ideas, and CareStream only helps with the second: a short check on your own medication policy. It does not sign anyone off.

items.q: Where does the quiz come from?
items.a: From your own policies. You pick the Medication topic module in the Training screen, and CareStream builds the lessons and questions from the policy text where it covers the topic, then general good practice. You edit and preview before assigning.

items.q: Can this replace medication administration training?
items.a: No. Practical medication administration training, including observed rounds, still needs a competent person. The check comes after the training day and shows who understood your policy. See the medication course for the certificate route.

items.q: What if a carer gets a question wrong?
items.a: It appears in their Follow-up tab. They can choose Learn & retry, a short lesson then a fresh question, or Just retry the same question, as often as they need. Treat it as information about the policy wording, and not as a mark against the carer.

items.q: Does my medication policy care home wording matter for this?
items.a: Yes. The check is only as good as your policy. If your medication policy care home document is vague on refusals or stock, the questions will reflect that. Use the results to spot where the wording needs to be clearer. You can find out-of-date policies too.

items.q: What does the law say about staff training and competence?
items.a: Regulation 12 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 requires that people giving care have the qualifications, competence, skills and experience to do so safely. Regulation 18 requires that staff receive appropriate support, training, professional development, supervision and appraisal. Neither tells you how to run a quiz.

items.q: What can I show an inspector?
items.a: You can show the questions, the lessons and the results together with your observation forms. That shows attendance, observed practice and understanding. Read about the compliance side and the questions inspectors put to staff.

items.q: Do I need a paid plan?
items.a: Adhoc training is on the paid plans, with a 14 day free trial. Create a free account on the registration page to look around first. Translation is also paid plans only.

guide.heading: A practical way to check understanding after medication training
guide.lede: Medication training for care staff does not end at the observed round. The round shows what a carer does while watched. The check for understanding shows whether they know what your own policy says.

sections.h3: Keep the assessor, add the check
paragraphs: Safe handling of medicines training works best in two parts. First, a competent person watches practice and signs it off. Second, you test the knowledge behind it, in your own words. The two answer different questions, and an inspector is likely to ask about both. The law asks that staff are competent, and that they receive appropriate training and supervision, so a record of each part helps you show how you meet that.

sections.h3: Four steps that fit a busy week
checklist: Within a few days of the training day: allocate the Medication topic module to the carers who attended, built from your own policy.
Before assigning: preview the questions and edit anything that does not match how your home works.
When an answer is wrong: the carer opens a short lesson on that point, then a fresh question.
Each month: look at the most missed questions and update the policy wording or your next training day.

sections.h3: What to do with the results
paragraphs: If many carers miss the same question, the policy may be unclear and the fix is the document, not the carers. If one carer keeps missing questions, that is a prompt for a supervision conversation and perhaps another observed round. Use the knowledge assessment to start that conversation, not to end it.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the observation forms, the questions, the lessons and the results together. That shows observed practice and understanding.
